module_title: Measuring, Cutting, and Preparing PVC Pipes

lessons.title: Accurate Measurement for Pipe Runs in Bathrooms and Kitchens
lessons.body: In bathroom and kitchen plumbing, a wrong measurement means wasted pipe, extra joints, and leaks. Start by understanding what you are measuring: pipe runs go from fitting to fitting, not wall to wall. For example, if you are connecting a sink P-trap to a wall drain, measure from the center of the trap outlet to the center of the drain pipe. Use a steel tape measure, not a cloth tape, because cloth stretches. Write down each measurement in millimeters. In many African markets, PVC pipes come in 3-meter or 6-meter lengths, so plan cuts to minimize waste. For a typical bathroom sink, the horizontal run from the wall to the P-trap might be 400 mm. Always measure twice: once at the actual location, and once after checking that the pipe will sit straight without forcing. Use a pencil or marker to mark the pipe where it will enter each fitting. Remember that fittings add length: a 90-degree elbow adds about 30-40 mm to the run. If you forget that, your pipe will be too short. For kitchen sinks, the run from the cabinet floor to the sink basket might be 600 mm vertical. Measure from the floor flange to the bottom of the basket strainer. Account for the slope: drain pipes need a fall of about 1 cm per 30 cm of horizontal run. So if your horizontal run is 900 mm, the end should be 30 mm lower than the start. Use a spirit level to check slope. In Africa, many homes have concrete walls, so you cannot easily move pipes inside walls. Measure from the outside of the wall to the fixture. Always add 10-20 mm extra on each end for insertion into fittings, then cut to final length after dry-fitting. Dry-fit all pipes and fittings before gluing. If a pipe is too long, you can cut more; if too short, you must start over. Keep a notebook with a sketch of the run, showing each measurement and fitting. This saves time and money.

lessons.title: Using a Hacksaw or Pipe Cutter for Clean Cuts on PVC
lessons.body: PVC pipe must be cut square, meaning the cut face is at exactly 90 degrees to the pipe length. A crooked cut causes leaks because the pipe will not seat fully in the fitting. You have two main tools: a hacksaw or a pipe cutter. A hacksaw is cheap and available everywhere in Africa. Use a 24-tooth per inch blade for PVC; too many teeth clog, too few chip the plastic. Secure the pipe in a vise or clamp it to a workbench. If you don't have a vise, use a G-clamp to hold it against a sturdy table. Mark the cut line all the way around the pipe with a pencil or marker. Then use a square (or a piece of paper folded to 90 degrees) to draw a line around the pipe. Start the cut with light strokes to make a groove, then use full strokes. Do not force the saw; let the teeth do the work. For a clean cut, rotate the pipe slightly after every few strokes. A pipe cutter (also called a plastic pipe cutter) works faster. It has a ratcheting mechanism and a sharp blade. Place the pipe in the cutter, tighten the handle until the blade touches the pipe, then rotate the cutter around the pipe while tightening slightly after each turn. Do not over-tighten or you will crack the pipe. The cutter makes a square cut with minimal burrs. For large diameters (50 mm and above), use a hacksaw or a mitre box. A mitre box helps keep the saw straight. After cutting, check squareness by standing the pipe on a flat surface; it should not wobble. If it wobbles, recut. Always wear safety glasses and gloves. PVC chips are sharp. In many African workshops, a hacksaw with a new blade costs less than a pipe cutter, but a pipe cutter saves time on many cuts. For a simple bathroom job, a hacksaw is fine. For production work, invest in a good pipe cutter. Remember: a clean cut saves you 10 minutes of deburring and prevents leaks.

lessons.title: Deburring and Chamfering Pipe Ends for Smooth Joints
lessons.body: After cutting PVC pipe, the cut edge has burrs: small ridges of plastic that stick out. If you don't remove them, the pipe will not slide fully into the fitting, and the solvent cement will not seal properly. Deburring means removing those burrs. Chamfering means making a slight bevel (angle) on the outside edge. Both are quick and essential. Use a deburring tool, a pocket knife, or a file. A deburring tool has a curved blade that shaves the inside and outside edges. If you don't have one, use a sharp knife to scrape the inside and outside edges at a 45-degree angle. Then use a file or sandpaper (80-120 grit) to smooth the edge. For chamfering, you want a bevel of about 1-2 mm on the outside edge. This helps the pipe slide into the fitting without pushing the cement out. A simple way: hold the pipe at a 45-degree angle and rub it on a piece of sandpaper or a file a few times. Do not over-chamfer; you don't want to reduce the wall thickness. After deburring and chamfering, wipe the pipe end with a clean rag to remove dust and plastic shavings. Then dry-fit the pipe into the fitting. It should go in easily but not loosely. If it is too tight, chamfer more. If too loose, the pipe may be out of round; you may need to cut a new end. In Africa, many plumbers skip deburring, but that leads to leaks. A leak in a wall means breaking the wall to fix it. Take 30 seconds to deburr and chamfer every pipe end. Use a rag to clean the inside of the fitting too. Solvent cement needs clean surfaces to melt and fuse the plastic. Any dust or oil weakens the joint. Keep a small deburring tool in your pocket. It costs little and saves hours.

lessons.title: Marking Insertion Depth for Solvent-Weld Joints
lessons.body: Solvent-weld joints (also called glue joints) work by melting the PVC surfaces and fusing them together. For a strong joint, the pipe must be inserted to the full depth of the fitting socket. If you insert too little, the joint is weak; too much, and the pipe bottoms out and may crack. So you must mark the insertion depth on the pipe. First, measure the depth of the fitting socket. For example, a 20 mm (1/2 inch) PVC elbow typically has a socket depth of about 15-20 mm. A 50 mm (2 inch) fitting has a depth of about 30-40 mm. Use a tape measure or a small ruler. Then, using a pencil or marker, draw a line around the pipe at that distance from the end. For example, if the socket depth is 20 mm, mark a line 20 mm from the cut end. When you insert the pipe into the fitting, you should see that line just at the edge of the fitting. This ensures full insertion. Some plumbers mark the pipe with a wrap of masking tape or a permanent marker. Do not use a grease pencil because it leaves residue. After marking, dry-fit the pipe and check that the mark aligns with the fitting rim. Then remove the pipe and apply solvent cement. Apply cement to both the pipe end (up to the mark) and the inside of the fitting. Push the pipe into the fitting with a quarter-turn twist. Hold for 30 seconds. The mark should disappear into the fitting. If the mark is still visible, you did not push hard enough. If the pipe bottoms out before the mark, the socket is shallower than you thought; recut and remark. In Africa, many leaks come from under-inserted pipes. A simple pencil mark prevents that. Keep a marker in your tool bag. Also, mark the pipe for orientation: draw a line along the pipe and fitting to align them. This helps when you have multiple joints. Always work quickly; solvent cement sets in seconds.

lessons.title: Avoiding Common Cutting Mistakes That Cause Leaks
lessons.body: Many PVC leaks are not caused by bad glue but by bad cuts. Here are the most common mistakes and how to avoid them. First, cutting at an angle. If your cut is not square, the pipe will not seat fully in the fitting. The cement will only touch part of the surface, leaving a gap. Always use a square or mitre box. Check squareness by standing the pipe on a flat surface. Second, not deburring. Burrs push the pipe out of the fitting or create a channel for water to leak. Always deburr and chamfer. Third, using the wrong blade. A hacksaw blade with too many teeth clogs and overheats the PVC, causing rough edges. Use 24 TPI. A dull blade smears the plastic. Change blades often. Fourth, cutting without measuring twice. If you cut too short, you waste pipe and may need a coupling. Always dry-fit before cutting. Fifth, not accounting for fitting depth. If you cut a pipe to the exact distance between two fittings, it will be too short because each fitting adds depth. Add the socket depth (e.g., 20 mm) at each end. Sixth, cutting on a dirty surface. PVC shavings and dirt get inside the pipe and contaminate the joint. Cut over a clean cloth or bucket. Seventh, using a wood saw. Wood saws have teeth that tear PVC. Use a hacksaw or pipe cutter. Eighth, cutting without clamping. If the pipe moves, the cut is crooked. Clamp it securely. Ninth, not marking the cut line all the way around. A partial mark leads to a crooked cut. Tenth, cutting pipe that is cold. In cold weather, PVC is brittle and cracks. Warm it slightly with your hands or leave it in the sun. In Africa, many of these mistakes happen because of rushing. Take your time. A clean, square, deburred cut is the foundation of a leak-free joint. Replace your blade when it starts to snag. Keep a file handy. And always test your joints with water before closing walls.

lessons.title: Practice Project: Cutting and Preparing a Simple Pipe Assembly
lessons.body: Now you will practice everything from this module by making a simple pipe assembly: a 90-degree elbow connecting two straight pipes. This is the most common joint in bathroom and kitchen plumbing. You will need: a 1-meter length of 20 mm PVC pipe, two 20 mm 90-degree elbows, a hacksaw or pipe cutter, a deburring tool or knife, sandpaper, a pencil, a tape measure, and PVC solvent cement. First, plan your assembly. Let's say you want a pipe that goes 300 mm up, then turns 90 degrees, then goes 200 mm horizontally. Measure and mark the first pipe: cut a piece 300 mm long. Remember to add insertion depth: each elbow socket is 20 mm deep, so cut the pipe 300 mm + 20 mm = 320 mm. Mark the cut line all the way around. Cut with a hacksaw, keeping the cut square. Deburr and chamfer both ends. Mark the insertion depth (20 mm) on each end. Repeat for the second pipe: 200 mm + 20 mm = 220 mm. Cut, deburr, chamfer, and mark. Now dry-fit the assembly: insert the first pipe into one elbow, then the second pipe into the other end of that elbow. Check that the marks align with the fitting rims. The assembly should look like an L shape. If any pipe is too long, recut. If too short, start over. Once dry-fit is correct, disassemble. Clean all surfaces with a rag. Apply solvent cement to the pipe end and inside the fitting. Push together with a quarter turn. Hold for 30 seconds. Wipe off excess cement. Repeat for the other joint. Let it cure for at least 1 hour before handling, and 24 hours before pressure testing. Test by blocking one end and filling with water. Check for leaks. If you see a leak, cut out the joint and redo it. This project teaches you measurement, cutting, deburring, marking, and gluing. Practice it three times. Each time, try to make the cuts cleaner and the joints stronger. In Africa, this simple assembly is used in almost every sink and shower installation. Master it, and you can build any pipe run.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Measuring, Cutting, and Preparing PVC Pipes

In African plumbing and construction markets â from Nairobi's Gikomba hardware corridor to Lagos's Ladipo pipe traders â the difference between a profitable job and a callback nightmare usually comes down to preparation. A solvent-welded PVC joint that leaks after handover costs you the pipe, the fittings, the labour, and often the client. This reference lesson consolidates the field knowledge you need to measure, cut, and prepare PVC pipes correctly the first time, so your business builds a reputation for work that holds.

PVC (polyvinyl chloride) is the dominant pressure and drainage pipe material across most African markets because it is cheap, chemically resistant, easy to work, and widely stocked. But it demands discipline: PVC does not tolerate sloppy cuts or rushed joints. This module gives you the numbers, the tools, and the checks that protect your margin.

Why Measurement Accuracy Drives Profit

Every millimetre of over-cut pipe is a fitting you cannot reuse, and every under-cut pipe is a joint that will not seat. In a bathroom or kitchen run, the most common failure is not the glue â it is the measurement. Pipe runs must account for fittings, wall thickness, and the insertion depth that each fitting consumes. A 90Â° elbow does not add zero length; it consumes a specific insertion depth at each end.

A practical rule used by experienced installers in Kenya and South Africa: measure the centreline run, subtract the fitting allowances, and cut 2â3 mm long, then trim to fit. This "cut long, trim to fit" approach is faster than re-cutting and protects your material budget.

Table 1: Insertion depth and fitting allowance for common PVC pipe sizes (solvent-weld, pressure-rated)
Nominal Pipe Size (mm) Min. Insertion Depth (mm) Recommended Cut Allowance per Joint (mm) Typical Use
201618â20Bathroom supply, small fixtures
251921â23Kitchen supply, branch lines
322224â26Main supply, riser lines
402628â30Main distribution
503133â35Drainage, large supply
633840â42Main drainage, industrial
754446â48Soil and waste stacks
1106062â65Main soil stacks, manholes

Source: Plastics Pipe Institute (PPI) Handbook of PVC Pipe, 5th Ed., Table 6-4 (Insertion Depth); and SANS 791 / EN 1452 fitting dimensions. Values are minimums â always confirm against the fitting manufacturer's data sheet.

Cutting Tools: Choosing the Right Method

On site, the two practical options are a fine-tooth hacksaw (24â32 TPI) or a rotary pipe cutter designed for plastic. A hacksaw is cheap and universal; a rotary cutter is faster and produces a squarer cut with less burr. For high-volume production work â say, prefabricating bathroom pipe sets for a housing project â a rotary cutter pays for itself in a week through reduced rework.

Table 2: Comparison of PVC cutting methods for field and workshop use
Method Cut Quality Speed Cost (USD, approx.) Best For
Fine-tooth hacksaw (24â32 TPI)Good, needs deburringMedium3â8Site work, small jobs
Rotary pipe cutter (plastic)Excellent, squareFast15â40Workshop, repeat cuts
Mitre saw with fine bladeExcellent, squareVery fast80â150Prefabrication, high volume
Angle grinder (not recommended)Poor, heat damageFast30â60Emergency only â risks cracks

Source: Adapted from the ASPE Plumbing Engineering Design Handbook, Vol. 1, and field data from Nairobi and Johannesburg plumbing suppliers, 2024. Costs are indicative and vary by market.

â  SAFETY WARNING â PVC CUTTING AND SOLVENT CEMENT

PVC dust and solvent cement vapours are hazardous. Always cut in a well-ventilated area, wear safety glasses and a dust mask, and never use solvent cement in a confined space without forced ventilation. Solvent cement is flammable â keep it away from open flames, sparks, and hot work. Wear nitrile gloves; PVC solvent cement can cause skin irritation and is harmful if inhaled. In African markets where workspace ventilation is often limited, take the cut outside or open both ends of the room before applying cement.

Deburring and Chamfering: The Step Most Installers Skip

After cutting, the pipe end has a burr on the inside and a sharp edge on the outside. If you do not remove these, three things happen: the burr scrapes cement off the fitting wall, the sharp edge pushes cement ahead of the pipe and creates a dry joint, and the pipe does not seat to full insertion depth. The result is a leak â often not immediately, but after the first pressure test or thermal cycle.

Deburr with a deburring tool, a pocket knife, or a file. Then chamfer the outer edge at 10â15Â° using a chamfering tool or a file. The chamfer should be about one-third of the wall thickness. This is not cosmetic â it is what allows the pipe to slide into the fitting without wiping away the cement.

Marking Insertion Depth

Before applying cement, dry-fit the joint and mark the insertion depth on the pipe with a pencil or marker. This mark tells you whether the pipe has seated fully. If the mark is still visible after assembly, the joint is not fully inserted and will leak. In high-volume work, a simple depth gauge or a pre-marked jig speeds this up dramatically.

Common Cutting Mistakes That Cause Leaks

From field experience across African plumbing contractors, these are the mistakes that generate callbacks:

  • Cutting at an angle: A bevelled cut reduces contact area and creates a stress point. Always use a mitre box or a square to guide the cut.
  • Not deburring: Burrs scrape cement and prevent full insertion.
  • Forgetting the chamfer: Without it, the pipe pushes cement out of the joint.
  • Measuring without fitting allowance: The pipe ends up short and the joint fails under pressure.
  • Using a dull blade: It cracks the pipe and leaves a rough edge.
  • Cutting in cold weather without warming: PVC becomes brittle below 5Â°C; warm the pipe slightly before cutting.
  • Not marking insertion depth: You cannot verify full seating.

Practice Project: Cutting and Preparing a Simple Pipe Assembly

Build a simple L-shaped assembly: two lengths of 25 mm PVC pipe joined by a 90Â° elbow. Measure the centreline run, subtract the elbow insertion allowance (19 mm each end), cut 2 mm long, deburr, chamfer, mark insertion depth, dry-fit, then solvent-weld. Pressure-test at 1.5Ã working pressure for 15 minutes. If it holds, you have the core skill for every bathroom and kitchen run.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Measure centreline run and subtract fitting insertion allowances.
  2. Cut 2â3 mm long, then trim to fit â never cut short.
  3. Use a fine-tooth hacksaw (24â32 TPI) or rotary pipe cutter.
  4. Deburr inside and outside edges immediately after cutting.
  5. Chamfer the outer edge at 10â15Â° (about one-third wall thickness).
  6. Dry-fit and mark insertion depth on the pipe.
  7. Clean both surfaces with PVC cleaner before cementing.
  8. Apply cement to both surfaces, insert fully, and hold for 30 seconds.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • Plastics Pipe Institute (PPI) â Technical documents and PVC installation guides
  • American Society of Plumbing Engineers (ASPE) â Plumbing Engineering Design Handbook excerpts
  • ISO 1452 â PVC-U piping systems for water supply (standard overview)
  • South African Bureau of Standards (SABS) â SANS 791 PVC pipe standards
  • Kenya National Environment Management Authority (NEMA) â construction waste handling guidance

Business takeaway: Accurate measurement, clean cuts, and proper end preparation are not extra steps â they are the difference between a one-day job and a three-day callback. In competitive African markets, your reputation for leak-free work is your best marketing. Train your team on this checklist, keep a deburring tool and a rotary cutter in every van, and your profit per job will rise while your warranty claims fall.

quiz.q: When measuring a pipe run from a sink P-trap to a wall drain, what should you measure between?
options: A) The outer edges of the pipes
B) The center of the trap outlet to the center of the drain pipe
C) The wall to the sink
D) The floor to the trap
quiz.explanation: Pipe runs are measured from center to center of fittings to ensure proper alignment and length.

quiz.q: Why should you use a steel tape measure instead of a cloth tape for plumbing measurements?
options: B) Cloth tapes stretch and give inaccurate readings
C) Steel tapes are easier to read
D) Cloth tapes are not available in Africa
quiz.explanation: Cloth tapes can stretch, leading to measurement errors, while steel tapes remain accurate.

quiz.q: What is the recommended fall (slope) for a horizontal drain pipe?
quiz.explanation: A fall of about 1 cm per 30 cm ensures proper drainage without allowing water to flow too fast.

quiz.q: Why must you dry-fit pipes and fittings before gluing?
options: B) To ensure correct length and alignment
quiz.explanation: Dry-fitting allows you to verify measurements and make adjustments before permanent gluing.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of using a pipe cutter over a hacksaw?
options: B) It makes a square cut with minimal burrs
C) It works on all pipe sizes
quiz.explanation: A pipe cutter produces a clean, square cut with fewer burrs, saving time on deburring.

quiz.q: How many teeth per inch (TPI) should a hacksaw blade have for cutting PVC?
quiz.explanation: A 24 TPI blade is ideal for PVC; too few teeth chip the plastic, too many clog.

quiz.q: What should you do if your cut pipe wobbles when stood on a flat surface?
quiz.explanation: Wobbling indicates a crooked cut; recutting ensures a square end for a proper joint.

quiz.q: What does deburring mean?
options: A) Making a bevel on the pipe
B) Removing burrs from the cut edge
C) Cleaning the pipe with solvent
quiz.explanation: Deburring removes the rough plastic ridges left after cutting.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of chamfering a PVC pipe end?
options: A) To make the pipe look neat
B) To help the pipe slide into the fitting without pushing cement out
quiz.explanation: A slight bevel allows smooth insertion and prevents the cement from being scraped off.

quiz.q: After deburring and chamfering, what should you do before dry-fitting?
options: B) Wipe the pipe end with a clean rag
quiz.explanation: Cleaning removes dust and shavings that could weaken the solvent weld.

quiz.q: Why is it important to mark insertion depth on a pipe before solvent welding?
options: A) To know where to cut
B) To ensure the pipe is inserted fully into the fitting
C) To align the pipe with the fitting
D) To measure the pipe length
quiz.explanation: The mark ensures the pipe reaches the full socket depth, creating a strong joint.

quiz.q: How do you determine the insertion depth for a fitting?
options: A) Measure the outside diameter of the pipe
B) Measure the depth of the fitting socket
C) Use a standard 10 mm for all fittings
quiz.explanation: The socket depth varies by fitting size; measuring it gives the correct insertion depth.

quiz.q: When applying solvent cement, which surfaces must be coated?
options: B) Only the inside of the fitting
C) Both the pipe end and the inside of the fitting
quiz.explanation: Coating both surfaces ensures a complete fusion and leak-free joint.

quiz.q: After pushing the pipe into the fitting with solvent cement, how long should you hold it?
quiz.explanation: Holding for 30 seconds prevents the pipe from backing out while the cement sets.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake that causes leaks in PVC joints?
options: A) Cutting the pipe too long
B) Not deburring the cut end
D) Marking the pipe with a pencil
quiz.explanation: Burrs prevent full insertion and create gaps that leak.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using a wood saw to cut PVC pipe?
options: A) Wood saws are too expensive
B) Wood saw teeth tear the PVC, causing rough edges
C) Wood saws are too slow
D) Wood saws cannot cut plastic
quiz.explanation: Wood saws have teeth designed for wood, which tear and crack PVC.

quiz.q: What should you do if you cut a pipe too short for your assembly?
options: A) Use it anyway with extra cement
B) Start over with a new piece
quiz.explanation: A too-short pipe cannot be fixed reliably; recutting a new piece is necessary.

quiz.q: In cold weather, why might PVC pipe crack when cut?
options: A) PVC becomes brittle in cold
D) The pipe is too hard
quiz.explanation: Cold makes PVC brittle, so it can crack instead of cutting cleanly.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the practice project of making a simple pipe assembly?
options: B) Plan the assembly and measure
quiz.explanation: Planning and measuring ensure you cut the correct lengths before any cutting.

quiz.q: In the practice project, if you want a 300 mm pipe with a 20 mm socket depth at each end, what total length should you cut?
quiz.explanation: Add 20 mm for each end: 300 + 20 + 20 = 340 mm.

quiz.q: After solvent welding, how long should you let the joint cure before pressure testing?
quiz.explanation: Full cure takes about 24 hours for maximum joint strength.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see a leak after testing your practice assembly?
options: A) Apply more cement on the outside
B) Cut out the joint and redo it
quiz.explanation: Leaks indicate a failed joint; cutting out and redoing is the proper fix.

quiz.q: Why is it important to mark the pipe for orientation when making multiple joints?
options: A) To know which end is which
B) To align the fittings correctly
D) To identify the pipe size
quiz.explanation: Orientation marks help keep fittings aligned as intended during assembly.

quiz.q: What tool can you use to check if a cut is square?
options: B) A square or folded paper
quiz.explanation: A square or a folded piece of paper at 90 degrees helps check squareness.

quiz.q: When using a pipe cutter, how should you tighten it?
options: B) Tighten slightly after each turn
C) Do not tighten at all
D) Tighten only at the end
quiz.explanation: Gradual tightening prevents cracking the pipe and ensures a clean cut.

quiz.q: What is the recommended grit of sandpaper for smoothing PVC pipe ends?
quiz.explanation: 80-120 grit is coarse enough to smooth without removing too much material.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid over-chamfering a pipe end?
options: A) It makes the pipe too short
B) It reduces wall thickness and weakens the joint
C) It makes the pipe too smooth
D) It causes the cement to dry too fast
quiz.explanation: Over-chamfering thins the pipe wall, compromising joint strength.

quiz.q: What should you do with the pipe after cutting but before dry-fitting?
quiz.explanation: Deburring, chamfering, and marking depth are all done before dry-fitting.

quiz.q: In the practice project, what shape does the final assembly make?
quiz.explanation: Two pipes connected by a 90-degree elbow form an L shape.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep a notebook with sketches of pipe runs?
options: B) To remember measurements and fitting positions
quiz.explanation: Sketches help avoid mistakes and ensure accurate assembly.
